description_full: Insulet Corporation develops, manufactures, and sells insulin delivery systems for people with insulin-dependent diabetes in the United States and internationally. The company offers Omnipod platform products comprising Omnipod 5 automated insulin delivery system, which includes a proprietary AID algorithm embedded in the pod that integrates with a third-party continuous glucose monitor to obtain glucose values through wireless Bluetooth communication; Omnipod DASH insulin management system that features a Bluetooth enabled pod that is controlled by a smartphone-like personal diabetes manager with a color touch screen user interface; and the Omnipod Insulin Management System. It also provides pods for Amgen for use in the Neulasta Onpro kit, which is a delivery system to help reduce the risk of infection after intense chemotherapy. The company sells its products to end-users through the pharmacy channel; and independent distributors. Insulet Corporation was incorporated in 2000 and is headquartered in Acton, Massachusetts.
ceo_bio: Ms. Ashley A. McEvoy | CEO, President & Director | Age 54 | Compensation: $3.1M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 5K people. Revenue per employee of $502K ranks in the above the sector median among Healthcare peers, improving at 23%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $70K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $12K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: Insulet Corporation is a large-cap healthcare business with a $10.2B market cap on $2.7B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +28% over the past three years and +24% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +3.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 62% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $378M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.30× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -10.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.0×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
